blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Questionnaire validation methodology is the staged process of developing or adapting an instrument and gathering evidence that its scores are valid and reliable in the target population.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: This section places the chapter’s tools in the order a validation study uses them. The COSMIN checklist (Mokkink et al., 2010) lists the measurement properties such a study should address: “internal consistency, reliability, measurement error, content validity (including face validity), construct validity (including structural validity, hypotheses testing and cross-cultural validity), criterion validity, responsiveness”. Use it to plan a study and to appraise published ones.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
A team develops a Hindi “CBHI trust” scale for rural Chhattisgarh.

  1. Define the construct and its domains from the literature and qualitative work.
  2. Draft items; content validity by an expert panel (§16.2.1).
  3. Translation and cultural adaptation when adapting an existing instrument. Beaton et al. (2000) set out five stages: at least two independent forward translations; a synthesis of the translations; back-translation into the source language by a translator “totally blind to the original version”; review by an expert committee; and a pretest of the prefinal version in the target population.
  4. Face validity and cognitive pretest in a small group of target respondents (§16.2.2).
  5. Field the draft to a validation sample.
  6. Structure and internal consistency. Use PCA or EFA to examine dimensionality (§16.5), then α per sub-scale with corrected item-total correlations and alpha-if-deleted (§16.3.1.1). Revise or remove items. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) then tests a pre-specified structure, ideally in a new sample. It is fitted as a structural equation model and is beyond this book.
  7. Test-retest reliability in a subsample (ICC(2,1) for the score, §16.3.2; weighted kappa for single ordinal items, §16.3.3.1), plus measurement error such as the repeatability coefficient.
  8. Build the composite score (§16.6).
  9. Construct validity by predefined hypotheses: convergent and discriminant correlations (§16.2.4.1) and known-groups comparisons, such as CBHI members against non-members (§16.2.4). Criterion validity if a gold standard exists (§16.2.3).
  10. Responsiveness, if the scale will measure change: “the ability of a questionnaire to detect clinically important changes over time, even if these changes are small” (Terwee et al., 2007). It is tested by giving the scale before and after an intervention expected to change trust.

points.html: Order. Statistical reliability checks (steps 6–7) should precede the interpretation of criterion and construct validity (step 9), because unreliability caps validity (§16.4). Design-stage evidence (content and face validity, steps 2–4) comes before any data.

Sample size. Terwee et al. (2007) consider “a sample size of at least 50 patients adequate” for assessing reliability and validity. For factor analysis, “rules-of-thumb vary from four to 10 subjects per variable, with a minimum number of 100 subjects”. These are conventions. A 20-item scale would need 80–200 respondents for EFA, and at least 100.
Iteration. Poor performance at any step (weak item-total correlations, low α, failed hypotheses) usually sends you back to revise specific items, not to abandon the instrument.

Validity is population-specific. Evidence applies to the population, language and setting in which it was gathered. An instrument validated elsewhere (for example, a Western quality-of-life scale) needs cross-cultural adaptation and fresh reliability and validity testing before use in rural Chhattisgarh.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 16.5

questions.prompt: A team runs PCA on 20 items meant to measure one construct, “quality of life”. Three components have eigenvalues above 1 (4.1, 1.3 and 1.1), explaining 20.5%, 6.5% and 5.5% of the variance. What do the percentages mean? What should the team check before concluding that the scale has three sub-dimensions?
questions.answer:
With 20 standardised items the total variance is 20. Each percentage is the eigenvalue ÷ 20: the first component carries 4.1 ÷ 20 = 20.5% of the total variance, the next two 1.3 ÷ 20 = 6.5% and 1.1 ÷ 20 = 5.5%.

The eigenvalue > 1 (Kaiser) rule is a convention that can keep too many components. Before concluding there are three sub-dimensions, the team should:

  • inspect the scree plot and run parallel analysis. Here the first component dominates, and the next two only just exceed 1;
  • look at the loadings. Does each extra component have several items loading highly, with a sensible theme (for example, all the social-relationship items)? Or is it one or two items, or a method artefact such as all the negatively worded items loading together?
  • check the result against theory (for example, the WHOQOL domains) and, ideally, confirm the structure by CFA in a new sample.

If the three components prove real, report α and build scores for each sub-scale, not one total.

questions.prompt: Explain why a highly reliable instrument is not automatically valid. A scale has reliability 0.64 and its criterion has reliability 0.81. What is the largest correlation the scale could show with the criterion?
questions.answer:
Reliability is consistency. An instrument can consistently measure the wrong thing, like a scale that always reads 2 kg high. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.

Largest possible correlation = √(r_xx × r_yy) = √(0.64 × 0.81) = √0.5184 = 0.72 (§16.4).

questions.prompt: A Hindi translation of an English depression scale is to be used in Raipur. List the translation steps, and name two measurement properties you would test afresh, with the statistic for each.
questions.answer:
Translation (Beaton et al., 2000): (1) two independent forward translations into Hindi; (2) synthesis of the two; (3) back-translation into English by a translator blind to the original; (4) expert committee review to agree a prefinal version; (5) pretest (cognitive interviews) in the target population.

Properties to test afresh, for example:

  • Internal consistency: Cronbach’s α per sub-scale, after checking structure by PCA/EFA (or CFA against the original structure).
  • Test-retest reliability: ICC(2,1), absolute agreement, over a suitable interval in at least 50 respondents (Terwee et al., 2007).
  • Criterion validity: sensitivity, specificity and AUC against a psychiatrist’s diagnostic interview.
  • Construct validity: predefined correlations, or known-groups comparisons (for example, attenders at a psychiatry OPD against community controls).
